hypotheses.claim: grunt-if is resolved in package-lock.json from the mutable git branch tarball URL https://github.com/binarymist/grunt-if/tarball/master (finding F-267, evidence E-1288), not from a registry version, so its content can change without any version change and builds are not reproducible; a compromise of that GitHub repo/branch would be pulled in silently. The package.json declaration string and Gruntfile.js usage could not be read directly (repository files are not readable by this agent), so those two parts are unverified.
reasons: E-1288 (guardian-rules GR-LOCK-001, package-lock.json:4407) shows the untrusted excerpt "resolved": "https://github.com/binarymist/grunt-if/tarball/master" — a mutable git branch tarball, not a registry version+integrity pin. E-1289 (dependency-graph) shows the node is in the real graph: owasp-nodejs-goat@1.3.0 > grunt-if@0.2.0, so the claim is about an actually-installed dependency, not a stray lockfile entry.

The claim's core inference — content can change without a version change, so builds are not reproducible and a compromise of that repo/branch would be pulled in silently — follows directly from a branch-tarball resolution and is not overstated.

Caveat recorded, not a rejection: the hypothesis itself states the package.json declaration string and Gruntfile.js usage were not read by the agent. Those two supporting details are therefore not part of the verified basis; the verdict rests on E-1288 and E-1289 alone, which is sufficient for the claim as written.

hypotheses.author: risk
hypotheses.claim: The Dockerfile base image is referenced as the mutable tag node:12-alpine (evidence E-1279 line 1 and E-1280 line 7) with no digest pin, so the base image content can change between builds; findings F-020 and F-021 are the same rule (GR-IMG-001) firing on the same Dockerfile and are duplicates of one another.
reasons: E-1279 (GR-IMG-001, Dockerfile:1) and E-1280 (GR-IMG-001, Dockerfile:7) both carry the excerpt "FROM node:12-alpine" with no @sha256: digest, supporting the mutable-tag / no-digest-pin claim exactly as written.

Both evidence records name the same rule ref GR-IMG-001 and the same file (Dockerfile), differing only in line (1 vs 7), which supports the duplicate characterization of F-020 and F-021 as one rule firing twice on one file rather than two independent weaknesses.
The claim is scoped to mutability of the base image reference and to the duplication; it does not assert that node:12-alpine is currently vulnerable, so there is no overstatement to reject.

hypotheses.author: risk
hypotheses.claim: GitHub Actions workflows reference third-party actions by mutable tags rather than commit SHAs: actions/checkout@v2 (E-1265, E-1266), actions/setup-node@v1 (E-1267, E-1268), actions/cache@v2 (E-1269, E-1270) and actions/upload-artifact@v2 (E-1271, E-1272) in .github/workflows/e2e-test.yml, and zizmor flags excessive-permissions (no explicit least-privilege permissions block) in e2e-test.yml (E-1264) and lint.yml (E-1273). A compromised or retagged action would execute in CI.
reasons: E-1264 (zizmor, excessive-permissions, .github/workflows/e2e-test.yml) shows the untrusted excerpt "overly broad permissions", supporting the missing least-privilege permissions block for e2e-test.yml; E-1273 is cited for the same rule in lint.yml.

E-1265/E-1266 (actions/checkout@v2), E-1267/E-1268 (actions/setup-node@v1), E-1269/E-1270 (actions/cache@v2) and E-1271/E-1272 (actions/upload-artifact@v2) are cited as file_location evidence for mutable tag references rather than commit SHAs.

The claim is correctly hedged: it says a compromised or retagged action *would* execute in CI, which is a conditional statement about the pinning practice, not an assertion that any of these actions is currently compromised. That is the right strength for tag-pinning evidence.

hypotheses.author: risk
hypotheses.claim: fsevents@1.2.9 is flagged as malicious by both grype (GHSA-xv2f-5jw4-v95m, E-0305) and osv-scanner (MAL-2023-462, E-0306) and declares a lifecycle install script (hasInstallScript: true, E-1287), so the malicious code would execute at npm install time; it is reached only transitively via forever@2.0.0 > forever-monitor@2.0.0 > chokidar@2.1.8 (E-0303) and is not imported by application code. F-001 and F-080 describe the same package and should be read together.
reasons: Supported at package level only: E-0305 (grype, ref GHSA-xv2f-5jw4-v95m, package-lock.json:3286) excerpt "Malware in fsevents" and E-0306 (osv-scanner, ref MAL-2023-462, same file/line) excerpt "Malicious code in fsevents (npm)", plus E-1287 (GR-INST-001, package-lock.json:3294) "hasInstallScript": true. That establishes a malware-flagged fsevents with a lifecycle script — nothing more.

(i) Overstated: the specific advisory-to-package tie for MAL-2023-462 is not in the excerpt. E-0306's excerpt names only "fsevents", not the advisory id; the id appears only in the record's ref field. The claim's framing that both scanners flag the same package with those two ids is not shown by the excerpts.

(ii) Overstated: "the malicious code would execute at npm install time" is not supported. The lockfile entry is optional and darwin-only, so it would not install on Linux CI, and no evidence record shows the install-script content was ever inspected. hasInstallScript: true proves a script exists, not that it is malicious or that it runs in this environment.

(iii) Overstated: "not imported by application code" is a reachability assertion; the available reachability signal is present_only, which does not establish non-import. E-0303's transitive path (forever@2.0.0 > forever-monitor@2.0.0 > chokidar@2.1.8) shows presence, not absence of use.

The underlying malware flag is real and worth reporting, but the exploitability conclusion as written goes beyond the cited evidence; a narrower claim limited to 'fsevents@1.2.9 is flagged as malicious by two scanners and declares an install script' would be supportable.

You previously recorded H-01 through H-04. Four further non-CVE supply-chain risks were reported by other agents from direct file reads, but you could not read repository files last time. Please TRY AGAIN to read the files (the paths are relative to the repository root: `package.json`, `Gruntfile.js`, `.dockerignore`, `Dockerfile`, `docker-compose.yml`, `.github/workflows/e2e-test.yml`, `.github/workflows/lint.yml`). If reads still fail, use `search_repo` / `run_anomaly_rules` / `inspect_lockfile_entry` instead, and only record a hypothesis if you obtain real tool evidence for it.

Claims to record (each narrowly worded, with the evidence ids you actually obtained):
a. `grunt-env` is declared in package.json as `"latest"` — a floating range — so installs are non-deterministic. (A prior agent reported package.json line 50.)
b. `Gruntfile.js` calls `grunt.loadNpmTasks("grunt-nodemon")` but `grunt-nodemon` appears in neither package.json nor package-lock.json — an undeclared dependency. (Prior agent reported Gruntfile.js line 147.)
c. The Dockerfile copies the whole build context with `COPY --chown=node . $WORKDIR` and `.dockerignore` does not exclude `.env`, so a developer's local `.env` would be baked into the image. (Prior agent reported Dockerfile line 13.)
d. The docker-compose `mongo` service uses the mutable tag `mongo:4.4` with no digest pin, and the CI workflows pull `mongo:4.0` by mutable tag at test time.

Also: if you can now read files, please re-check and strengthen H-01 (the grunt-if mutable tarball) with the package.json declaration string and the Gruntfile.js usage line, and update its claim/evidence accordingly.

Return: the ids of any new hypotheses created, their one-line claims and evidence ids, and an explicit list of any claim you could NOT record because no tool evidence was obtainable. Also report the current total finding count and any new findings created if you re-ran build_findings.

Two small, targeted tasks on repository TARGET OWASP__NodeGoat-20261123T184721Z. Do not start broad investigations.

TASK 1 — Narrow hypothesis H-04. The verifier REJECTED H-04 as overstated. Its exact supported wording is:
"fsevents@1.2.9 is reported as malware by both grype and osv-scanner (E-0305, E-0306) and declares a lifecycle install script (E-1287); it is reached only transitively via forever@2.0.0 > forever-monitor@2.0.0 > chokidar@2.1.8 (E-0303), is an optional darwin-only dependency, and the script content was not inspected. It also carries CVE-2023-45311 / GHSA-8r6j-v8pm-fqw3 (CVSS 9.8, F-016)."
Please update H-04 to exactly this narrower claim (or as close as the tool allows), keeping evidence refs E-0303, E-0305, E-0306, E-1287 and finding ids F-001, F-080, F-016. The verifier's key corrections: (i) the specific advisory-to-package tie for MAL-2023-462 is NOT demonstrated in the evidence — only the package-level "malware in fsevents" excerpt is; (ii) "malicious code would execute at npm install time" is unsupported because the lockfile shows `"optional": true` and `"os": ["darwin"]` (lines 3295–3298), so it would not install on Linux CI; (iii) "not imported by application code" is not evidenced — reachability is only `present_only`. Remove all three overstatements.

TASK 2 — Record ONE new hypothesis for the grunt-if supply-chain risk if and only if you can obtain real tool evidence. H-01 is already verified and covers the mutable tarball URL. Do NOT duplicate it. Instead, only if you have evidence, record a hypothesis that `grunt-if` is a devDependency loaded by Gruntfile.js at build time, so the mutable-branch risk affects developer/CI build machines rather than the production runtime image (the Dockerfile runs `npm install --production`). If you cannot get evidence for the Gruntfile usage, do not record it — just say so.

Return: the updated H-04 claim text and its status, whether any new hypothesis was created (with id), and confirmation that no other hypotheses were altered.

reasons: E-1279 (GR-IMG-001, Dockerfile:1) and E-1280 (GR-IMG-001, Dockerfile:7) both carry the excerpt "FROM node:12-alpine" with no @sha256: digest, supporting the mutable-tag / no-digest-pin claim exactly as written.

Both evidence records name the same rule ref GR-IMG-001 and the same file (Dockerfile), differing only in line (1 vs 7), which supports the duplicate characterization of F-020 and F-021 as one rule firing twice on one file rather than two independent weaknesses.
The claim is scoped to mutability of the base image reference and to the duplication; it does not assert that node:12-alpine is currently vulnerable, so there is no overstatement to reject.

E-1288 (guardian-rules GR-LOCK-001, package-lock.json:4407) shows the untrusted excerpt "resolved": "https://github.com/binarymist/grunt-if/tarball/master" — a mutable git branch tarball, not a registry version+integrity pin. E-1289 (dependency-graph) shows the node is in the real graph: owasp-nodejs-goat@1.3.0 > grunt-if@0.2.0, so the claim is about an actually-installed dependency, not a stray lockfile entry.

The claim's core inference — content can change without a version change, so builds are not reproducible and a compromise of that repo/branch would be pulled in silently — follows directly from a branch-tarball resolution and is not overstated.

Caveat recorded, not a rejection: the hypothesis itself states the package.json declaration string and Gruntfile.js usage were not read by the agent. Those two supporting details are therefore not part of the verified basis; the verdict rests on E-1288 and E-1289 alone, which is sufficient for the claim as written.

E-1264 (zizmor, excessive-permissions, .github/workflows/e2e-test.yml) shows the untrusted excerpt "overly broad permissions", supporting the missing least-privilege permissions block for e2e-test.yml; E-1273 is cited for the same rule in lint.yml.

E-1265/E-1266 (actions/checkout@v2), E-1267/E-1268 (actions/setup-node@v1), E-1269/E-1270 (actions/cache@v2) and E-1271/E-1272 (actions/upload-artifact@v2) are cited as file_location evidence for mutable tag references rather than commit SHAs.

The claim is correctly hedged: it says a compromised or retagged action *would* execute in CI, which is a conditional statement about the pinning practice, not an assertion that any of these actions is currently compromised. That is the right strength for tag-pinning evidence.

Supported at package level only: E-0305 (grype, ref GHSA-xv2f-5jw4-v95m, package-lock.json:3286) excerpt "Malware in fsevents" and E-0306 (osv-scanner, ref MAL-2023-462, same file/line) excerpt "Malicious code in fsevents (npm)", plus E-1287 (GR-INST-001, package-lock.json:3294) "hasInstallScript": true. That establishes a malware-flagged fsevents with a lifecycle script — nothing more.

(i) Overstated: the specific advisory-to-package tie for MAL-2023-462 is not in the excerpt. E-0306's excerpt names only "fsevents", not the advisory id; the id appears only in the record's ref field. The claim's framing that both scanners flag the same package with those two ids is not shown by the excerpts.

(ii) Overstated: "the malicious code would execute at npm install time" is not supported. The lockfile entry is optional and darwin-only, so it would not install on Linux CI, and no evidence record shows the install-script content was ever inspected. hasInstallScript: true proves a script exists, not that it is malicious or that it runs in this environment.

(iii) Overstated: "not imported by application code" is a reachability assertion; the available reachability signal is present_only, which does not establish non-import. E-0303's transitive path (forever@2.0.0 > forever-monitor@2.0.0 > chokidar@2.1.8) shows presence, not absence of use.

The underlying malware flag is real and worth reporting, but the exploitability conclusion as written goes beyond the cited evidence; a narrower claim limited to 'fsevents@1.2.9 is flagged as malicious by two scanners and declares an install script' would be supportable.
